newsitem.title: LEBANON: Low Lebanon turnout threatens Hizbollah.
newsitem.headline: Low Lebanon turnout threatens Hizbollah.

text.p: Low turnout on Sunday in the eastern Bekaa valley appeared to threaten the pro-Iranian Hizbollah with a new setback in the final round of voting in Lebanon's parliamentary election.

Shortly after polls closed at 5:00 p.m. (1400 GMT) the interior ministry said a preliminary count showed that about 37 percent of the 410,000 voters cast their ballots. Results were expected on Monday.
The Bekaa is a stronghold of Hizbollah, which has military training camps in the valley for its guerrillas who are fighting Israeli troops in a south Lebanon border strip.
It was electing the last 23 members to the 128-member parliament after voting in Mount Lebanon, the north, Beirut and the south on the past four Sundays.
The Lebanese Association for the Democracy of Elections (LADE), an independent watchdog, reported many irregularities in the poll. It reported widespread abuses in the earlier rounds.

A pro-government list including six ministers, several parliamentary deputies and candidates of Hizbollah and the secular Amal, Lebanon's two main rival Shi'ite Moslem movements, was expected to win most of the seats.
It was challenged by a 10-man leftist ticket headed by communist party leader Farouk Dharouje and a six-man list of independents.

The low turnout appeared to threaten the chances of a Maronite Christian and a Sunni Moslem candidate that Hizbollah (Party of God) was backing on the pro-government list beside three of its own candidates, local poll observers said.
Hizbollah lost two of its eight parliamentary seats in earlier rounds and losses by two supporters in the Bekaa would be another damaging blow.
Hizbollah was due under deals engineered by Syria to win the election of a total of seven deputies and two supporters compared with eight deputies and four supporters in the previous parliament.
Hizbollah's Sunni supporter could lose because he was facing popular Sunni rivals on other lists, observers said.
Christians, who total over 25 percent of Bekaa voters, were either refusing to vote or were crossing Hizbollah and its supporters off their ballot papers, they said.
Reporters at polling stations saw many people holding ballot papers with Hizbollah candidates crossed off.
"Hizbollah candidates are being deleted. We still don't know how widely practised this has been but there is evident deletion of our candidates' names," Hizbollah deputy Khodr Tleis told reporters.
Local observers said Bekaa Christians were angry because a Maronite Christian on the pro-government list was chosen by Hizbollah under an election deal brokered by Syria.
They were also showing dislike for President Elias Hrawi, a pro-Syrian Maronite from the Bekaa. Hrawi's son Roy failed to win election at the last elections in 1992.

Syria has 35,000 troops in Lebanon and a large presence in the Bekaa. Local politicians say it intervened to engineer the makeup of the pro-government list to prevent politicians it dislikes from being elected and to avert an open fight between Amal and Hizbollah in the predominantly Shi'ite region.
